title: What can actually determine the deformation parameters α and β?
summary: The recovered user fragment asks about α and β and gives approximately 0.0334 and 0.673. Two numerical constants alone do not imply a mathematical relationship. A useful replacement is an identification problem with an explicit observation model and a dimensionless input.
definitions: For x>0, write d(x)=αx^β, with α>0 and β real.
If X has units of length, α has units length^(1−β) in X+αX^β. A dimensionless convention is X*=X_P[u+a u^β], u=X/X_P, with dimensionless a.

result.name: Two-point identifiability
result.statement: Two exact positive correction measurements d1=d(x1), d2=d(x2), with x1≠x2, determine β=log(d2/d1)/log(x2/x1) and α=d1/x1^β uniquely.
result.proof: Taking logarithms gives log di=log α+β log xi. Subtracting the two equations eliminates log α; the nonzero denominator log(x2/x1) permits division. Substitution then gives α. Conversely, the resulting pair satisfies both observations, so existence and uniqueness hold. With noisy observations, the same transformation becomes linear regression, but its errors are logarithmic errors, not necessarily additive errors in the original units. One observation gives the entire curve α=d1x1^(−β), so it cannot distinguish exponents. A short input range makes log(x2/x1) small and amplifies measurement errors. This is a conditioning issue that extra printed decimal places do not resolve.

example.setup: Take x1=1, x2=8, d1=1/30 and d2=2/15. These are exact model data for an illustrative exponent rather than historical measurements.

title: A sublinear signed deformation is a homeomorphism, with a cusp at zero
summary: The historical radial correction becomes a precise real-variable map once its sign and parameter range are fixed. It is invertible for every α>0 and 0<β<1, but its derivative is unbounded near zero. This distinction matters whenever the map is inserted into a differential equation or metric.
definitions: Let φ(x)=x+α sign(x)|x|^β and φ(0)=0.
A map is inverse 1-Lipschitz when |φ⁻¹(u)−φ⁻¹(v)|≤|u−v| for all u,v.

result.name: Global inversion and regularity
result.statement: For α>0 and 0<β<1, φ is an increasing homeomorphism R→R. Its inverse is 1-Lipschitz. The map φ is smooth off zero and fails to have a finite derivative at zero.
result.proof: The signed power s(x)=sign(x)|x|^β is continuous and strictly increasing. Thus for y>x, φ(y)−φ(x)=(y−x)+α[s(y)−s(x)]≥y−x>0. This proves injectivity and the inverse Lipschitz inequality. The limits at positive and negative infinity are respectively positive and negative infinity; continuity and the intermediate value theorem give surjectivity. A continuous strictly monotone bijection has a continuous inverse. For x≠0, φ′(x)=1+αβ|x|^(β−1)>1. At zero, φ(h)/h=1+α|h|^(β−1), which diverges as h→0. Consequently a smooth change-of-variables theorem requiring a finite nonzero derivative cannot be invoked at zero. There is a useful local Hölder estimate as well: for0<β<1, the signed power is β-Hölder with constant at most2^(1−β). On a bounded interval, φ therefore has a quantitative modulus of continuity even though it is not Lipschitz at zero. This separates continuity, differentiability and inverse stability.

example.setup: Take α=1/3 and β=2/3. Evaluate at x=−8,0,8 and examine the inverse close to zero.
example.calculation: φ(8)=8+4/3=28/3 and φ(−8)=−28/3. For small y, y≈α sign(x)|x|^β, hence φ⁻¹(y)≈sign(y)(|y|/α)^(1/β)=sign(y)(3|y|)^(3/2). The exact inverse inequality bounds any recovered-input error by the output error.
example.conclusion: The transformation is globally well behaved for inversion, while differentiating it at its cusp requires separate treatment. These are compatible facts.

limits: The later logistic-factor formula X+α|X|^βF(X/X_P) is a different function and has not been substituted into this proof. Its negative-input behavior and monotonicity require their own analysis.
extension: For an equation in the transformed variable, first derive its weak or integral form. Then state whether trajectories cross zero; a formal chain rule at the cusp can otherwise introduce a nonexistent derivative.

title: A genuine deformed algebra requires transported operations
summary: The recovered framework applies a common deformation to many algebraic objects. A rigorous interpretation is transport of structure: a bijection can re-express a known algebra without changing its identities. Merely replacing symbols by starred symbols does not determine a new multiplication.
definitions: Let φ:R→R be a bijection. Define x⊕y=φ⁻¹(φ(x)+φ(y)) and x⊙y=φ⁻¹(φ(x)φ(y)).
The transported zero is z=φ⁻¹(0), and the transported unit is e=φ⁻¹(1). Scalar coordinates are part of the definition.

result.name: Transport gives an isomorphic field
result.statement: The operations ⊕ and ⊙ make R into a field isomorphic to the ordinary real field by φ. In particular, associativity and distributivity are exact, irrespective of whether φ is linear.
result.proof: Apply φ to (x⊕y)⊕w. The result is (φ(x)+φ(y))+φ(w), which equals φ(x)+(φ(y)+φ(w)); injectivity of φ proves associativity. Similarly φ(x⊙(y⊕w))=φ(x)(φ(y)+φ(w))=φ(x)φ(y)+φ(x)φ(w)=φ((x⊙y)⊕(x⊙w)). The remaining field axioms follow by the same argument, with additive inverse φ⁻¹(−φ(x)) and multiplicative inverse φ⁻¹(1/φ(x)) when x≠z. This proof also explains its limit: no new intrinsic field invariant appears, because φ is an explicit isomorphism. Geometry, norms or differentiation added afterward may change, but they need independent definitions. For the cubic example the transported additive inverse remains−x, but the transported sum is not ordinary addition. Its scalar action must likewise be transported: c acting onx becomesφ⁻¹(cφ(x)) if the scalar field itself is left in ordinary coordinates. Mixing these two scalar conventions would create a different structure.

example.setup: Use φ(x)=x³, a simple exact bijection that avoids numerical inversion.
example.calculation: x⊕y=(x³+y³)^(1/3), whereas x⊙y=xy. Thus 1⊕1=2^(1/3). Both (1⊕1)⊕(−1) and 1⊕(1⊕(−1)) equal1. Ordinary addition combined with an arbitrary corrected product would not be covered by this calculation.
example.conclusion: The example supplies an exact associative deformation, with a completely explicit explanation of what has and has not changed.

limits: Transport through a coordinate bijection is not a proof that a proposed starred Lie algebra, magic square or mass formula has new representation theory. For vector spaces or noncommutative algebras, one must specify a bijection on the entire underlying set and transport all relevant operations.
extension: Test a proposed new multiplication by computing its associator on a basis. If it is transported, exhibit the isomorphism; if it is not, prove the identities directly and identify an invariant distinguishing it from the starting algebra.

title: Constant width is a condition on the support function
summary: The geometry in the recovered framework becomes testable when width is expressed through a support function. This also separates a body’s radial distance from the distance of its supporting line, quantities that generally differ.
definitions: For a convex body K, h(θ)=max{x·(cosθ,sinθ):x∈K} is its support function. Its width in direction θ is h(θ)+h(θ+π).
A twice continuously differentiable h with h+h″>0 parameterizes a strictly convex curve by x(θ)=h(θ)n(θ)+h′(θ)t(θ).

result.name: An explicit family and an obstruction
result.statement: The support function h(θ)=1+εcos3θ has constant width2 and is strictly convex for |ε|<1/8. Applying h↦h+αh^β, with α>0 and 0<β<1 and nonzero sufficiently small ε, generally destroys constant width.
result.proof: Because cos(3(θ+π))=−cos3θ, the sum h(θ)+h(θ+π)=2. Differentiating twice gives h+h″=1−8εcos3θ, which is positive under the stated bound; the curve formula then has positive radius of curvature. For the nonlinear correction, write c=cos3θ. The new width is2+α[(1+εc)^β+(1−εc)^β]. At c=0 it is2+2α. At c=1 strict concavity of u^β yields (1+ε)^β+(1−ε)^β<2, so the width is strictly smaller. Equivalently its Taylor expansion starts2+2α+αβ(β−1)ε²c²+O(ε⁴). The nonconstant second-order term is an explicit obstruction. The support-function curve formula also explains closure: both h andh′ are2π-periodic, so the parameterized endpoints agree. Translating the body adds a first harmonic a cosθ+b sinθ to h; this preserves width because that harmonic is odd under the antipodal shift. The third harmonic changes shape without merely translating it.

example.calculation: The curvature radius lies between1/2 and3/2, so the starting curve is safely convex. Its original width is exactly2. The corrected widths at c=0 and c=1 differ by (1/30)[(17/16)^(2/3)+(15/16)^(2/3)−2], which is negative by strict concavity.
example.conclusion: The proposed universal correction does not preserve constant width even on a small smooth family. A preservation theorem needs an odd-antipodal support perturbation.

title: An irrational angular frequency does not define a closed polar curve
summary: The recovered “irrational monogon” series must first pass a periodicity test. A formula on the real angular line is not automatically a function on the quotient circle R/(2πZ). Without that descent, closing the curve and assigning its homology are extra operations.
definitions: A function r:R→R descends to S¹ precisely when r(θ+2π)=r(θ) for all θ.
For positive continuous periodic r, the map θ↦r(θ)(cosθ,sinθ) is a polar graph.

result.name: A one-mode obstruction
result.statement: For a≠0 and ξ>0, r(θ)=1+a cos(ξθ) is 2π-periodic if and only if ξ is an integer. For irrational ξ, the endpoints of its restriction to [0,2π] have different radial distances.
result.proof: If r is periodic, evaluate at θ=0 to obtain cos(2πξ)=1, hence ξ is an integer. Conversely an integer frequency is periodic by the cosine addition formula. For irrational ξ, cos(2πξ)≠1, so r(2π)−r(0)=a[cos(2πξ)−1]≠0. The same polar direction at the two endpoints therefore has different radii. This proof does not automatically classify infinite sums: different frequencies can cancel, and their coefficients must be examined. It does show that irrationality by itself is not a mechanism producing a closed “one-sided” polygon. One may instead study an almost-periodic function on R, or add a closing segment, but those choices define different spaces. If a closing segment is explicitly added, the resulting loop can be studied, but its geometry depends on that segment. An endpoint identification in the parameter interval is a quotient construction instead and may fail to give a continuous planar map when the two endpoints have different images. These are distinct repairs.

example.setup: Take r(θ)=1+(1/4)cos(√2θ). It stays between3/4 and5/4, so the issue is not passage through the origin.
example.calculation: r(0)=5/4, while r(2π)=1+(1/4)cos(2π√2)≠5/4. The polar arc therefore has a nonzero endpoint gap of magnitude (1/4)|1−cos(2π√2)|. Replacing √2 by3 makes the endpoint gap zero and produces a threefold periodic radial graph.
example.conclusion: A continuous nonclosed arc and a simple closed curve have different topological models. The model must be chosen before computing homology.

limits: This is a necessary-definition correction, not a proof that every irrational-frequency infinite series is nonperiodic. Nor does it preclude studying nonperiodic angular curves as legitimate objects.
extension: For a finite trigonometric sum with distinct positive frequencies, prove linear independence of exponentials to determine exactly which coefficients can survive a prescribed period. Then specify whether the domain is R, an interval or S¹.

title: Regularity of the recovered lacunary angular series
summary: A meaningful infinite angular construction needs a convergence theorem. The same coefficients that control its size do not necessarily control its slopes: each differentiation multiplies the nth oscillation by ξ^n. This gives an explicit hierarchy of sufficient conditions.
definitions: Let ξ>1 and r(θ)=1+Σ_{n≥0}a_n cos(ξ^nθ).
For k≥0, put M_k=Σ_{n≥0}|a_n|ξ^(kn), allowing the value infinity.

result.name: A sufficient regularity criterion
result.statement: If M_k is finite for an integer k≥0, the series defines a C^k function on R. Every derivative of order j≤k is obtained term by term and is uniformly bounded by M_j.
result.proof: The jth derivative of a_n cos(ξ^nθ) has absolute value at most |a_n|ξ^(jn). Since ξ>1 and j≤k, finiteness of M_k implies finiteness of M_j. The Weierstrass uniform convergence test therefore applies to every derivative series through order k. To justify differentiation, fix a base point and integrate the uniformly convergent first derivative series: the fundamental theorem of calculus identifies its integral with the uniform limit of the original partial sums. Repeating this argument proves the result through order k. The criterion is sufficient only. Failure of absolute summability of derivative bounds does not by itself prove nondifferentiability, because cancellation can matter. For k=0 the uniform tail bound is sup|Σ_(n>N)a_n cos(ξ^nθ)|≤Σ_(n>N)|a_n|. In the first geometric example this equals(1/16)(1/8)^(N+1)/(1−1/8). Thus every plotted truncation has a certified amplitude error, independently of sampling density on the angular line.

example.setup: Choose a_n=2^(−3n−4), ξ=2, and n starting at0. Compare it with a_n=2^(−n−4).
example.calculation: For the first choice, M_0=(1/16)/(1−1/8)=1/14 and M_2=(1/16)/(1−1/2)=1/8. Hence r≥13/14 and r is C² with |r″|≤1/8. For the second, M_0=1/8 but the first derivative majorant is Σ1/16, which diverges; the theorem guarantees continuity but supplies no C¹ conclusion.
example.conclusion: The first series is a quantitatively controlled positive radial function. The second needs additional analysis before slopes or curvature can be used.

extension: Once periodicity is established, combine the derivative bounds with an explicit curvature formula for a polar graph to identify a rigorously convex parameter range.

title: Homology follows from a specified space, not a deformation name
summary: The historical rank formula needs a definition of κ and a construction of the underlying space. Two elementary models expose the issue: a finite graph has computable cycle rank, whereas every positive continuous periodic radial graph is a single topological circle.
definitions: A finite graph has V vertices, E edges and C connected components; homology here uses integer coefficients.
A positive radial graph is Γ={r(θ)(cosθ,sinθ):θ∈S¹} with continuous r>0.

result.name: Two exact homology models
result.statement: For a finite graph, H0≅Z^C, H1≅Z^(E−V+C), and higher homology vanishes. A positive continuous radial graph has H0≅Z and H1≅Z.
result.proof: Orient the graph edges. Its boundary map ∂1:Z^E→Z^V sends an oriented edge to head minus tail. On each connected component, a spanning tree supplies V_component−1 independent boundary columns; all columns lie in the subgroup whose coordinate sum on that component is zero. Thus rank ∂1=V−C. There are no 2-cells, so H1=ker∂1, a free group of rank E−V+C; H0 is the component group. For Γ, the polar parameterization is a continuous bijection from compact S¹ to a Hausdorff space: positivity makes its inverse the angular projection. It is therefore a homeomorphism, and the usual circle homology applies. Subdividing a graph edge increases both E and V by one and leaves E−V+C unchanged. This is an elementary consistency check for the claimed invariant: changing the mesh of a polygonal approximation should not create a new cycle merely by inserting vertices. Adding an actual closing edge can change the rank.

example.setup: Compare a circle with a connected graph consisting of two circles meeting at one vertex.
example.calculation: The one-vertex, one-loop circle has V=1,E=1 and β1=1. The wedge of two circles has V=1,E=2 and β1=2. Inserting a continuous positive factor r*(θ)/r(θ) in a radial graph changes neither its one-to-one angular parameterization nor β1.
example.conclusion: To obtain rank κ−1, one can specify a connected graph with E−V+1=κ−1. The formula is then a graph theorem rather than a consequence of an irrational exponent.

limits: Self-intersections, quotient identifications, added closing arcs or singularities can change the space. They require an explicit cell complex; the simple radial-graph proof does not apply to them.
extension: Build the proposed construction as a finite cellular approximation, list its incidence matrices, and compute their integer Smith normal forms. This separates actual topology from pictures of an oscillatory parametrization.

title: What persistence stability can certify for a deformation
summary: Persistence becomes precise after choosing both a space and a filtration. The most elementary useful theorem is a pair of sublevel-set inclusions. It supplies a stable comparison without assuming the homology of an undefined geometric object.
definitions: For a fixed space X and a function f:X→R, let F_t={x:f(x)≤t}.

result.name: Uniform perturbations yield an interleaving

The composite inclusion F_t→G_(t+ε)→F_(t+2ε) sends each point to itself, so functoriality makes its induced homology map equal the structure map H_k(F_t)→H_k(F_(t+2ε)). The other composite works identically. This is the definition of an ε-interleaving at the level of persistent homology. For finite filtered complexes, additional algebraic results identify this with a bottleneck matching bound on interval decompositions; that stronger correspondence is a classical theorem, not proved merely by drawing similar curves.

title: A complete small sheaf calculation before spectral-sequence claims
summary: The recovered passage names sheaf spectral sequences without specifying a sheaf or cover. A two-set calculation gives the missing data and shows exactly where first cohomology comes from. The example uses the constant real sheaf on a circle.
definitions: Cover S¹ by two connected proper open arcs U,V whose intersection has two connected components.
Locally constant real sections on a space with m connected components form R^m.

result.name: The circle Čech calculation
result.statement: For this cover and the constant real sheaf, the Čech complex is R²→R², (a,b)↦(b−a,b−a), in degrees0 and1. Its cohomology is R in each of degrees0 and1, and zero above1.
result.proof: A section on each connected arc is a single number, so degree0 is R⊕R. A section on U∩V can take independent values on its two components, so degree1 is R⊕R. Restriction subtracts the U-value from the V-value on both components, producing the displayed differential. Its kernel is the diagonal line a=b, and its image is the diagonal line in degree1. Thus H0 has dimension1 and H1 is R² modulo a one-dimensional diagonal, also dimension1. There are no triple intersections of distinct cover members, so higher Čech groups vanish. Because the arcs and their intersection components are contractible and acyclic for this sheaf, this cover computes the sheaf cohomology. The acyclicity is part of why this particular cover is useful.

example.setup: Take the degree1 cochain c=(1,0). Determine whether it is a coboundary.
example.calculation: Every coboundary has equal coordinates, so c cannot equal(b−a,b−a). Its class is nonzero. The quotient can be identified with R by the difference map (u,v)↦u−v; c maps to1. A class represented by(5,4) is the same class because their difference(4,4) is a coboundary.
example.conclusion: The nontrivial class records incompatibility between the two overlap components. There is no need to infer it from an undefined “deformed” spectral sequence.

title: Hochschild homology and K-theory detect different data
summary: Naming several invariants does not make them interchangeable. An exact matrix example supplies two computable definitions and shows why a topological-cycle rank cannot simply be reused as a Hochschild or K-theory rank.
definitions: For a complex algebra A, HH0(A)=A/[A,A], where [A,A] is the linear span of commutators xy−yx.
For a unital C*-algebra, K0 is the group completion of stable projection classes. For complex matrix algebras these classes are classified by ordinary rank after stabilization.

result.name: An explicit matrix calculation
result.statement: HH0(M₂(C))≅C via trace, whereas K0(M₂(C))≅Z via stable rank. With the rank-one projection as generator, the unit matrix has K0-class2.
result.proof: Trace annihilates every commutator, since Tr(XY)=Tr(YX). Conversely, write Eij for matrix units. The off-diagonal units satisfy E12=[E11,E12] and E21=[E22,E21], while E11−E22=[E12,E21]. These three matrices span the traceless subspace. Hence the commutator span is exactly the kernel of trace, so the quotient is one-dimensional and trace identifies it with C. For K0, a complex projection is unitarily diagonalizable with diagonal entries0 or1. Under direct sum, ranks add. Every nonnegative rank occurs among matrix algebras over M₂(C), and equality of rank gives stable equivalence. The resulting monoid is N and its group completion is Z. The identity in M₂(C) has rank2, explaining the normalization of its class. The trace used in the Hochschild quotient is unnormalized, so the identity matrix maps to2. A normalized trace would send it to1 and change the numerical comparison with K0, without changing either invariant group. This small normalization choice is another reason to state a proposed comparison map explicitly.

summary: The September 10 assistant claim gives no usable definition or asymptotic proof of a deformed Benford law for elliptic coefficients. A sound formulation reduces leading digits to fractional logarithms and proves an exact model where equidistribution is available.

title: Unitary evolution does not make neighboring states orthogonal
summary: The recovered discussion mentions temporal orthogonality but the relevant formula is truncated. A two-dimensional example settles the basic issue: unitarity preserves inner products between jointly evolved states, but does not make a trajectory orthogonal to itself at every later time.

summary: The recovered inequality is a standard atomic estimate once the function has mean zero. Omitting cancellation materially changes the theorem. The normalization can be proved in one line, but specifying the ambient real Hardy space and the atom conditions is essential.
definitions: On R^d, an L² Hardy atom supported in a ball B has integral0 and L² norm at most |B|^(−1/2).
